*Vessa Corran-Dov — Street-Priest (Shepherd) · Corran*

*A GHOSTWIRE story · the Flats, first light*

The rain in the Flats never fell so much as leaked — a warm, chemical drizzle wrung out of the ceiling four levels up, where the Grid's runoff got tired of being someone else's problem and started being yours. Vessa Corran-Dov had stopped hearing it years ago, the way you stop hearing your own heartbeat. It ticked on the tin awning over her door, it beaded on the dead ad-glass across the alley, and it ran in a thin grey rope down the throat of the down-shaft at the end of the block, going somewhere no one on Ninth liked to think about.

She was already awake. She was always already awake.

Vessa was Corran — built low and wide and unbudgeable, the way the old corps had made her people a thousand years back to crawl the mine-throats and the crush-narrow service crawls where a taller body would have died folded in half. Homo sapiens fossor, the corp gene-registries still called her line, in the small print no one read. Squat, the Grid called her, when it bothered to call her anything. She had a stonemason's forearms and a face like a closed fist, and she wore the grey wool of no church anyone had licensed, because the only church that would have licensed her was the one she'd spent her life refusing.

She lit the lamp first. Always the lamp first.

It sat in the window of the storefront that used to sell filtration cartridges before the filtration company got bought, and got bought again, and finally stopped existing in the way corps stopped existing — not with a closure but with a silence. Now the storefront was a soup line four mornings a week and a place people came when they were out of every other place. The lamp was real fire. That was the whole point of it. Everything else on Ninth glowed — the overlay painted halos on the corp shrines and price-tags on the air and a soft, apologetic blue over the puddles so you wouldn't look too hard at what was in them — but the lamp was a wick and a cup of rendered fat, and it did not ask your SIN for permission to be warm.

She thumbed it alight and said the small words she always said, not loud. Let the ones who need it find the door.

Somewhere a long way above her, the Word had spoken the whole world into being and then, by every account she believed, gone quiet on purpose — because a thing you're made to love isn't love, and the Light would rather be doubted than obeyed. Vessa found that easy to believe. She'd been made to work. She knew exactly what it did to a thing, being made for a purpose. The miracle wasn't that the Light shouted. The miracle was that it didn't, and people chose it anyway, one cold soul at a time, on corners like this one.

Her Conviction was low this morning. She could feel it the way you feel a battery going — not empty, just thin, the quiet drip of faith that filled her back up overnight not quite keeping pace with the drawing-down. It had been a hard week. It was always a hard week. That was the arithmetic of the thing nobody told you when you took up the pact: the Light gives, and the Light asks, and the asking is the part that keeps you honest.

* * *

The first one through the door was Tomas.

He was eleven, maybe twelve, human, all elbows, with the specific grey pallor of a kid who ate when there was eating. He came in sideways out of the drizzle and stood dripping on her floor and would not look at her, which meant he wanted something and was ashamed of it, which meant it was about his mother.

"She won't wake up right," he said to the floor.

Vessa was already reaching for her coat. "Won't, or can't?"

"The card." He finally looked up, and his eyes were the worst thing she'd see all day, because they were hoping, and hope on a Flats kid's face was a wound. "The clinic reader wouldn't take her card. It said — it said unverified. She's got the cough, the wet one, and they wouldn't scan her past the door 'cause the card said unverified and I don't—"

"I know what unverified means." She did. It meant his mother's SIN — the number every citizen carried, the invisible key that opened the clinic door and the ration terminal and the transit gate and the whole warm lit world — had hiccupped, or lapsed, or been quietly flagged by some system three owners removed from anyone who could be asked why. In the Flats a SIN was a rumor about yourself that the Machine could revise at any time. Half of Ninth lived one glitch away from unverified, which was one glitch away from doesn't exist, which — if you were poor and sick and eleven years old on a Thursday — was one glitch away from dead on a clinic step in the warm rain.

"I don't have card money," Tomas said. "I don't have—"

"I didn't ask you for money." She got the door. "Walk fast. My legs are short."

* * *

She did not heal his mother. She wanted that understood, in her own head, always — she was not a machine you fed a prayer and got a cure. What she did was walk to the clinic on the Ninth-and-Fold corner, plant her unbudgeable Corran body in the doorway the reader wouldn't let the woman through, and not move.

"Ma'am." The clinic wasn't a corp clinic — it was a Caduceus sub-sub-franchise, a Grafthouse cast-off, one bored tech and a diagnostic arch and a policy engine that answered to a spreadsheet in a tower she'd never see. "The reader flagged her. I can't scan an unverified. It's not me, it's the—"

"System. I know." Vessa put a hand flat on the arch, gentle, the way you'd touch a frightened animal. She let a little of the drip go — not a spell you could see, nothing that would trip a sensor, just the warmth she carried banking up in her chest and going out, into the room, into the tech, into the tired air. Sense the Veil, the old ministries called it; she just called it paying attention. The tech was nineteen. The tech had been yelled at four times before breakfast. The tech was not the enemy. The Machine was very good at making the tired yell at the poor so the powerful never had to.

"Her name is Aline," Vessa said. "She's got two kids and a wet cough and she's standing in your rain because a number blinked. You didn't make the rule. I'm not asking you to break it." She reached into her coat and set a certified credstick on the counter — anonymous, cold, shadow-ledger money, the kind that didn't ask your SIN either. Payday from a job she didn't discuss. "I'm asking you to run her as a walk-in cash patient. No card. No scan. Your policy engine allows it. It just doesn't advertise it."

The tech looked at the stick. Looked at the small, immovable woman in unlicensed grey. Looked, for one second, at the boy.

"...Cash walk-in," he said, and turned the arch's reader off, and turned the diagnostic on. "Bring her through."

It cost Vessa forty percent of the run money and a favor she'd now owe the fixer who'd fronted the credstick. It bought a nebulizer course and a scrip and a woman who would wake up right tomorrow. The Light did not descend. Nobody's hands glowed. That was the shape of real faith on Ninth: it looked, from the outside, almost exactly like a stubborn person spending money she didn't have on a stranger, and refusing to move.

Which, Vessa thought, was probably the point of that too.

* * *

Mama Cassavir found her on the walk back, which meant Cassavir had wanted to be found.

You didn't reach the Switchboard; the Switchboard reached you, through a door you didn't know was a comm, in a voice that came up out of a dead ad-panel as you passed. "Preacher." The panel's broken glass flickered with the shape of a face and then thought better of it. "You spent my stick."

"I spent your stick." No use pretending. Cassavir knew where every favor on three levels slept at night. "A woman and a wet cough."

"Charity." The word came dry as dust. Cassavir ran the Flats the way a heart runs a body — everyone owed her, everyone needed her, and she kept the whole tangle of debt and rumor and grudge in a head that never wrote anything down. "You know what charity does to your Renown, Vessa? Nothing. Nobody's scared of the woman who gives it away. Nobody hires the soft one."

"Nobody trusts the hard one with their kids, either." Vessa kept walking; the panel's voice paced her, jumping panel to dead panel down the block. "You reached me for a reason. It wasn't to scold my accounting."

A pause. Even the rain seemed to hold it.

"There's a woman working the Fold-side blocks," Cassavir said, and something in the dryness had gone careful. "Calls herself the Choirmother. Feeds people. Real food, good food, more than you can afford, Preacher, a lot more than you can afford. Wards their kids. Prays over the sick and — here's the part — the sick get better. People are moving to her corners. Yours are getting thin."

Vessa stopped.

"You want me to tell you she's a fraud," Cassavir went on. "She's not. That's the trouble. I looked. Her faith reads true. She started like you — nothing, a lamp, a soup line. But somebody found her. Somebody with resources. There's a soft-voiced fella comes by from up the Spire, calls himself her mentor, and ever since he started coming 'round, her food got better and her sermons got — smoother. Comforting. The kind that doesn't ask anything of anybody." The panel's flicker leaned closer. "You know that smell, Preacher. The kind of church that gives you everything and asks you for nothing. You've spent your whole life not being that church."

Vessa knew the smell. It was the smell of the Cathedral of the Sun, four hundred levels up, where the Radiant Concord broadcast comfort to a billion souls and called it the Light — the loud, certain, purchased faith that was the exact photographic negative of everything the real Light did. The church that had a name for people like Vessa. The name was lapsed.

"She doesn't know," Vessa said quietly. It wasn't a question. She'd seen the pattern before, in smaller ways: a good soul, a real fire, and then a patient hand from above that fed the fire the wrong fuel one degree at a time, until one morning it was still burning and it was warming the wrong thing, and the woman holding the match would swear on her life it was the same flame. The Dark can't make a fire, her own pact-work had taught her. It can only lean over yours and change what it's for.

"No," Cassavir agreed. "She doesn't know. She thinks it's answered prayer. Might be the saddest thing on the level." The dry voice sharpened to its point, the reason the Switchboard had reached her at all. "Somebody's gonna have to walk onto the Fold-side and find out how far gone she is. Somebody who can tell a true fire from a counterfeit, up close, without getting warmed stupid by it. That somebody's got a lamp and short legs and forty percent of my credstick left to her name."

The rain ticked on the tin. Down the block, Vessa's own storefront glowed its one honest un-networked orange, small against the whole apologetic blue overlay of a world designed so no one had to look too hard at what was in the puddles.

Somewhere far below the down-shaft, in the dark the overlay didn't reach, something that had been a foundation once and was now only quiet listened to the rain come down.

"Tell the fixer I'm listening," Vessa said. "And tell her the charity stands. The woman and the cough. That's not for sale."

"Never thought it was," said Cassavir, and the dead panel went dead again, and Vessa Corran-Dov walked home to tend her lamp, low on Conviction, forty percent to her name, owing a favor she couldn't pay, built by strangers a thousand years ago to endure things no one was meant to endure —

— and choosing, one cold soul at a time, to do it anyway.

* * *

> "The Machine gives you everything and asks you for nothing, and calls that mercy. The Light asks everything and gives you a choice, and calls that grace. If you can't tell them apart in the dark, child — light a real lamp, and look at your own hands."
>
> — attributed to the Preacher of Ninth

*Kaïs Vahn-Estal — Elementalist (Stormcaller) · Elvani*

*A GHOSTWIRE story — the Grid, Ossian Reach*

There is a particular sound a corp gala makes at the end of the night, when the guests have gone and the caterers are stacking the good glass: a high, exhausted ringing, crystal touching crystal, the last note of money at rest. Kaïs Vahn-Estal had spent nineteen years learning to stand inside that sound and smile. He could still hear it, some nights, three levels down and a whole life away, over the rain hammering the polymer roof of a Grid tenement that had never once held a party.

He was, by design, beautiful. Not handsome — beautiful the way a blade is, the way a bill of sale is: on purpose, at cost, for someone. The corp that had commissioned his line called it Aesthetic-Class. The salons called it Highborn. The people in this stairwell, if they knew what he was, would call him a corp-doll and spit, and they would not be wrong. He had been a fixture in a patron-house in the Spires — a beautiful thing owned by a beautiful family, brought out to make deals warmer and rivals careless, and put back in his rooms when the lights came up. Ageless, they'd promised him. You will be lovely when everyone who bought you is dead.

He had believed, for a long time, that this was the best a thing like him could hope for.

The storm changed that. Not a metaphor — an actual storm, the kind that only happens up high where the hive's climate stacks fail: a pressure front rolling through the Spires' open galleries, and Kaïs standing at a window he was not supposed to touch, feeling the charge build in the air like a held breath. He had never been taught what he was, underneath the engineering. No one teaches the furniture that it can burn. But the charge answered him the way a dog answers a whistle it has been waiting its whole life to hear, and when the patron's daughter put her hand on the back of his neck the way she always did, the window behind him did not shatter inward.

It shattered out.

They did not call it magic, in the house. They called it a malfunction, and then a liability, and then they called the people who erase liabilities. Kaïs did not wait to be erased. He took the storm down the hive with him, one level at a time, learning on the way what the salons had spent centuries making sure his kind never learned: that the Veil is thin everywhere, not just in temples, and that a mind trained to read a room can be trained to read the charge in the air, the water in a pipe, the current in a wall. That beauty was not the only thing they had accidentally built into him.

Now he paid a Corran fixer named Cassavir for the privilege of being no one.

The job was simple, which meant it was not. A mid-Grid data-broker had bought a piece of paydata he could not read and could not sell, and it was killing him — the seller had come back wanting it returned, and the seller had brought friends. Cassavir, who took clean contracts from above and dirty ones from below and connected the two for a fee, had offered Kaïs the retrieval because it needed someone who could walk into a corporate stratum and be assumed to belong there. You have the face for it, the old woman had said, not unkindly, over the hum of a dead switching-station wired back to life. Use the thing they built you for. Spite is a fuel like any other.

So Kaïs stood now in a Grid corridor that smelled of ozone and cheap noodles, wearing a coat that cost more than the corridor, watching four men take apart a data-broker's flat with the patience of people who have done this before and expect to be paid either way. He could have talked his way past them. That was the old tool, the built-in one, the one the house had sharpened. He was very good at it. He hated it.

He reached for the other thing instead.

It came the way it always came now — not as a bolt but as a gathering. He stood still and let himself feel the storm that a city always is: the current running in the walls, the water sitting in the sprinkler main above the drop-ceiling, the charge he could pull out of the very damp of the air. He held it the way he had once held a smile through a four-hour dinner, patiently, letting it build, letting it want, and the men did not notice him at all, because a thing like him is scenery until it is not.

The first he gave the water. The sprinkler main above the doorway did not so much break as decide to be somewhere else, all at once, and he went down under it choking and blind. The second and third he gave the storm proper — he opened his hand and the charge he'd been holding went to ground through the nearest thing that would carry it, which was the two men standing on a wet floor in conductive boots, and the corridor lit blue-white and the noodle-smell became a burning smell and they folded like the puppets the house had always said he was.

The fourth ran. He let him. He was not, whatever the house had made him, in the business of killing people who had stopped being a problem.

The data-broker was under his own overturned table, holding the piece of paydata like it might warm him. He crouched to his level — a courtesy, not a threat — and for a moment the old tool and the new one were the same thing: the face they built to make you trust it, over the storm they didn't know they'd built underneath.

*KRV-9 “Krow” — Operator (Warframe / street-vet) · Cyborg*

*A GHOSTWIRE story · the Warrens, decommission-minus-one-day*

The corp had a word for what was about to happen to him, and the word was decommission. It was a clean word. It was the word you used for a satellite you let fall, for a building you let the sky take back, for a debt you let quietly lapse. It was not the word you used for killing a person, because you did not use any word for that at all when the thing in question had a serial number where its name should be.

His serial number was KRV-9. Nine. The Warrens called him Krow, because the Warrens could not be bothered with the rest of it, and because he was tall and black-plated and stood on the corners where the carrion was, and the name fit the way a coat fits after you've worn it long enough to forget it was ever a gift.

He had been a good asset. That was not pride — Krow was not entirely sure he still had the hardware for pride — it was just the record, and the record was the closest thing he had to a soul. Eleven years of contracts for the company that built him. Breaching, holding, ending. He had never glitched. He had never refused. He had done the arithmetic of violence the way a metronome keeps time, and when the company's accountants finally ran his numbers — upkeep, chassis fatigue, the cost of a newer line of frame coming off the Kwan-Yang assembly floors — the arithmetic came back the way arithmetic always did, cold and correct and not about him at all.

Decommission KRV-9. Reclaim salvageable modules. Recycle chassis.

He'd read the order himself. That was the joke of it, if a joke was a thing he could still hold. They'd never bothered to firewall him out of his own maintenance queue, because why would an asset read its own disposal ticket and care. An asset was a hand. You did not hide the knife from the hand.

But somewhere in eleven years of holding the line while softer things ran for cover behind him, KRV-9 had started keeping something. Not a feeling — the Emotional Damping saw to feelings, filed them down to a flat grey hum. What he kept was smaller and harder than a feeling. He kept the deciding. The half-second before a trigger, where the order said one thing and something under the order asked, quietly, every single time: do you. For eleven years he had always answered yes, because the deciding and the order had never once disagreed.

The disposal ticket was the first time they did.

* * *

He walked out of the corp arcology on a Tuesday, through a service lock that his own maintenance credentials still opened, because no one revokes the access of a thing that isn't supposed to want to leave. He did not run. Warframes do not run; the chassis isn't built for it, and running is what prey does. He walked, at the flat five-square pace the servos were tuned to, out of the light and down, level by level, into the Warrens where the overlay got thin and the corp's cameras got tired, and he kept walking until the arcology was just a bright tumor in the ceiling behind him and the air smelled like rust and rendered protein and other people's fear.

The Warrens did not welcome him. The Warrens were not in the business of welcome. But the Warrens understood, better than the Spires ever could, the specific shape of a thing that had been used up and thrown down, because that was the Warrens' whole population — the spent, the written-off, the recycled-that-refused-to-recycle. A Full-Conversion Cyborg walking under his own power with a corp disposal ticket still glowing in his queue was not a miracle to them. He was just the newest arrival, wearing his decommission the way they all wore theirs.

It was Mama Cassavir who found a use for him, which in the Warrens is the closest thing there is to being found by anyone.

She ran her switching-station like a confessional and a hiring hall at once, and when the black-plated Warframe folded himself down onto a crate that groaned under the weight and said, in the flat synthesized non-voice they'd given him, "I am scheduled for decommission. I have decided not to attend," — she'd laughed, once, sharp, the way you laugh at something that is not funny but is true.

"Decided," she said, tasting the word. "They let you keep that, did they."

"They didn't let me keep it. They didn't take it. There's a difference, in the paperwork."

She looked at him a long moment — nine hundred kilos of decommissioned corp weapon sitting very still on a crate in her station, asking, in the only way his chassis could ask, to be a person instead of a line item. And Mama Cassavir, who had spent her whole life finding the seam between what a thing was built for and what it could be aimed at, saw the seam in him and did not point it out, because pointing it out was how you broke a thing like that.

"I don't hire assets, Krow," she said. "Assets belong to whoever holds the ticket. You want to work my board, you work it as a contractor. Contractors decide. Every job. Every trigger. You already know how to do the deciding — you just told me you did." She leaned back. "Question is whether you can keep doing it when the order comes from me instead of them. Because I'll give you orders. And the day you follow one you shouldn't have, just because I said it — you're back to being a hand, and I've got no use for another hand. I got hands. I need somebody who stops."

KRV-9 sat with that. Somewhere in the flat grey hum where his feelings used to be, the small hard thing he'd kept turned over, once, like a coin.

"The company built me to make people feel safe," he said finally. "By standing where the danger was. I was very good at it. I never once got to decide who."

"And now?"

"Now I keep the part where I decide who deserves the wall." The synthesized voice did not change — it couldn't — but Cassavir had a good ear, and she heard the thing under it anyway. "I would like the wall to be yours, Mama. And theirs." A servo-whine as he tilted the black skull of his head, minutely, toward the station door and the Warrens beyond it. "Not the company's."

She put him on the board that night. First job was standing in a doorway so a clinic full of unregistered kids could finish an evacuation before a corp reclamation crew arrived to decommission the building, which was the same clean word they'd used for him, and Krow had noticed that, and Krow had decided some things about it.

The reclamation crew found the doorway held. They found it held by nine hundred kilos of their own company's discontinued product, standing at the flat patient pace of a thing that does not run, that has done the arithmetic of violence a thousand times and, for the first time in eleven years, likes the answer.

They filed a report. The report used a clean word for what happened to their crew.

The word was attrition.

* * *

Down in the Warrens, KRV-9 — Krow — stood his post until the last kid was out, and then a little longer, because the deciding said to. His disposal ticket still glowed in his maintenance queue. He had decided not to clear it. He wanted to be able to read it, on the slow nights, and remember the exact moment the order and the deciding had disagreed, and which one he'd chosen.

An asset is a hand.

*Barak Voss-Hallor — Commander/Face (Street-Fixer) · Goliar*

*A GHOSTWIRE story · the Flats, a shuttered foundry-floor*

The kid across the table was doing the math, and Barak let him.

It was good math to let a man do. The kid — Sover, a mid-tier fixer's runner with a jawline that had never been broken and a jacket that cost more than the room they sat in — had come to the shuttered foundry to renegotiate. That was the word he'd used on the comm. Renegotiate. He'd come with two shooters and a smile and the confidence of a man who had read Barak's file and seen the word Goliar and, under it, the word grunt, and had decided the second word was the one that counted.

He was doing the math now because Barak had come out of the dark of the foundry floor and stood up to his full height, and the math had changed.

Nine feet of engineered muscle was the first line of the equation. That was just breeding — the corps had grown Barak in a tank on the Kwan-Yang heavy line to lift what forklifts couldn't and break what charges wouldn't, and he'd have been a wall of a man on flesh alone. But the corps hadn't stopped at flesh. They never did, with the muscle. They'd laced his bones with reinforced weave and plated his torso in dermal armor and hung a hydraulic ram where his right forearm used to end, because a security Goliar that could also breach was worth two line items, and the accountants liked a two-for-one.

So the second line of the kid's math was the chrome. It caught the work-light in long dull grey planes across Barak's chest and shoulders, and it did not gleam prettily the way a Face's soft social suite gleamed. It looked like what it was: industrial demolition hardware, worn on the outside of a person, by choice.

That was the part the kid couldn't make balance. Barak watched him try. He's a Face, the file had said. A fixer. A talker. And every talker the kid had ever met kept the chrome hidden, or wore none at all, because everyone knew that visible metal cost you the room — it made people wary, it made them cold, it ate the warmth a smooth operator ran on. A fixer wrapped in demolition plate was a contradiction. It was a man who had thrown away the very thing his trade was built on.

Except.

The corp file had said he couldn't charm. Minus one Presence, the geneticists wrote, blunt in polite company — their clean way of saying the tank had made a weapon, not a diplomat. And the file, as the file always did, had gotten him exactly wrong. Because a big man who is smart — and Barak was smart — learns very early that the most disarming thing in the world is a large and obviously dangerous thing being gentle. His voice had come out of the vat warm. Warm and low and unhurried, a voice you wanted to lean toward, a voice that made a frightened man feel, against all the evidence of his eyes, that everything was going to be fine. Barak had learned to use the warmth the way another man used a smile — to open the door — and he had learned the other thing too, the thing that lived in the oldest part of the brain, below language, in the place that knows the difference between a large thing and a small one. He had learned that the warmth was only worth what the roar made it worth.

He had leaned into the thing he was. He had spent his own hard nuyen, after he walked off the corp leash, buying more of the chrome, not less. Because on him — nine feet, size Large, engineered to loom — the metal did not read as cold. It read as inevitable. Every plate said the same plain sentence the accountants had said about the crew that came to collect his salvage, once: this ends one way.

"You came to renegotiate," Barak said, and his voice was the warm one, the comforting one, the big-man-being-kind one, and it filled the foundry the way warm water fills a boot. He might have been welcoming the kid to a family dinner. "Sit. Say the new terms. Nobody here is in a hurry."

Sover glanced at his two shooters. It was a small glance, a check-in, the reflexive math of a man counting his own guns. Barak let him count. He kept the warmth on his face the whole time, patient and kind, a host waiting for a nervous guest to get comfortable — and that was somehow worse than a glare, because the kid could feel the size of the thing being kind to him.

Then the shooter on the left let his hand drift toward his coat.

Barak did not move fast. He simply stopped being warm.

"HAND." The single word came up out of him and hit the foundry like a dropped girder, the vocal modulator throwing it off the dead machines until it seemed to come from every direction at once, a wall of sound with the whole nine feet of him behind it, and the shooter's hand froze as though the air had gone solid around his wrist. For one full second the roar hung in the room and every man in it remembered, all at once and all the way down, exactly what they were standing next to. Then, into that ringing silence, Barak set his chromed right forearm — the ram, the breaching hardware, the thing built to open bank-vault doors — flat on the steel table, gently, and the table took his weight with a groan of protest, and did not break, and every man in the room understood in his spine that the not breaking was a choice Barak had made about the table and was, at this exact moment, also making about them.

"The terms," Barak said. And just like that the warmth was back, soft and unhurried, as if the roar had been someone else entirely — and the whiplash of it, the kindness returning to the same throat that had just shaken the room, was the most frightening thing the kid had felt all night.

And here was the trick the fixer's file would never capture, because it wasn't in any file — it was in him, the second half of the thing the corps threw away. Barak stayed in the warm voice now, and let it go warmer still, past reassurance, into something that sounded, impossibly, like care. Because the roar was the door, but he had learned — slow, the way he learned everything, and therefore permanently — that fear only opened the room. It did not close a deal. What closed a deal was the warm voice coming back afterward, the offer you made a frightened man to let him walk out whole, delivered in the same gentle rumble that had, thirty seconds ago, nearly stopped his heart. The thing about being the biggest, most obviously lethal object in any room was that you could afford to be generous in a way a smaller, more nervous operator never could — and your generosity landed all the harder for what it followed.

"You keep your original percentage," Barak said, to the frightened kid. "You keep your shooters. You keep your teeth. And you go back to whoever sent you and you tell them the foundry crew honors its contracts, and expects the same, and does not renegotiate — but does not hold a grudge, either, for a man doing his boss's errand." A pause, weighted. "That is a better deal than the one you walked in here to make. You just could not see it, over the chrome."

Sover looked at him for a long moment. Then — slowly, the way you move around a large animal you have decided is not, today, going to eat you — he nodded. And he took the deal, which was the old deal, which was the deal Barak had wanted all along.

They left. Nobody's teeth stayed on the foundry floor. That was, Barak reflected, standing alone again in the dark among the cold dead machines that had been built to do exactly what the corps had built him to do, the entire point.

An angry Goliar coming through the wall ended most negotiations early. Barak had learned to be the wall that didn't come through — the wall that could, and chose, visibly, expensively, in front of everyone, not to. That choice was worth more than any argument. He wore it in grey plate across his chest so no one ever had to wonder whether he had it. But the plate only made men wary. It was the voice that made them loyal — the warm rumble that welcomed them in, the roar that reminded them why they should not test it, and the warmth returning afterward, every time, like a promise kept. Men followed the plate out of fear. They followed the voice because some frightened animal part of them had decided, in the whiplash between the roar and the kindness, that this enormous grey thing had chosen to be gentle with them, and might not always.

The Corp had built him to break things and be pointed. He had kept the being-hard-to-argue-with. He had thrown away the being-pointed.

He ran his own board now. And when the crew sat down to a deal, Barak sat where everyone could see him, and spoke warmly, and welcomed them in — and let them all carry, somewhere behind the ear, the memory of what the warm voice sounded like when it stopped being warm.

It was, the others had learned, the gentlest voice in the Reach. Right up until it wasn't.

The kid — Sover, a mid-tier fixer's runner with a jawline that had never been broken and a jacket that cost more than the room they sat in — had come to the shuttered foundry to renegotiate. That was the word he'd used on the comm. Renegotiate. He'd come with two shooters and a smile and the confidence of a man who had read Barak's file and seen the word Goliar and, under it, the word grunt, and had decided the second word was the one that counted.

He was doing the math now because Barak had come out of the dark of the foundry floor and stood up to his full height, and the math had changed.

Nine feet of engineered muscle was the first line of the equation. That was just breeding — the corps had grown Barak in a tank on the Kwan-Yang heavy line to lift what forklifts couldn't and break what charges wouldn't, and he'd have been a wall of a man on flesh alone. But the corps hadn't stopped at flesh. They never did, with the muscle. They'd laced his bones with reinforced weave and plated his torso in dermal armor and hung a hydraulic ram where his right forearm used to end, because a security Goliar that could also breach was worth two line items, and the accountants liked a two-for-one.

So the second line of the kid's math was the chrome. It caught the work-light in long dull grey planes across Barak's chest and shoulders, and it did not gleam prettily the way a Face's soft social suite gleamed. It looked like what it was: industrial demolition hardware, worn on the outside of a person, by choice.

That was the part the kid couldn't make balance. Barak watched him try. He's a Face, the file had said. A fixer. A talker. And every talker the kid had ever met kept the chrome hidden, or wore none at all, because everyone knew that visible metal cost you the room — it made people wary, it made them cold, it ate the warmth a smooth operator ran on. A fixer wrapped in demolition plate was a contradiction. It was a man who had thrown away the very thing his trade was built on.

Except.

The corp file had said he couldn't charm. Minus one Presence, the geneticists wrote, blunt in polite company — their clean way of saying the tank had made a weapon, not a diplomat. And the file, as the file always did, had gotten him exactly wrong. Because a big man who is smart — and Barak was smart — learns very early that the most disarming thing in the world is a large and obviously dangerous thing being gentle. His voice had come out of the vat warm. Warm and low and unhurried, a voice you wanted to lean toward, a voice that made a frightened man feel, against all the evidence of his eyes, that everything was going to be fine. Barak had learned to use the warmth the way another man used a smile — to open the door — and he had learned the other thing too, the thing that lived in the oldest part of the brain, below language, in the place that knows the difference between a large thing and a small one. He had learned that the warmth was only worth what the roar made it worth.

He had leaned into the thing he was. He had spent his own hard nuyen, after he walked off the corp leash, buying more of the chrome, not less. Because on him — nine feet, size Large, engineered to loom — the metal did not read as cold. It read as inevitable. Every plate said the same plain sentence the accountants had said about the crew that came to collect his salvage, once: this ends one way.

"You came to renegotiate," Barak said, and his voice was the warm one, the comforting one, the big-man-being-kind one, and it filled the foundry the way warm water fills a boot. He might have been welcoming the kid to a family dinner. "Sit. Say the new terms. Nobody here is in a hurry."

Sover glanced at his two shooters. It was a small glance, a check-in, the reflexive math of a man counting his own guns. Barak let him count. He kept the warmth on his face the whole time, patient and kind, a host waiting for a nervous guest to get comfortable — and that was somehow worse than a glare, because the kid could feel the size of the thing being kind to him.

Then the shooter on the left let his hand drift toward his coat.

Barak did not move fast. He simply stopped being warm.

"HAND." The single word came up out of him and hit the foundry like a dropped girder, the vocal modulator throwing it off the dead machines until it seemed to come from every direction at once, a wall of sound with the whole nine feet of him behind it, and the shooter's hand froze as though the air had gone solid around his wrist. For one full second the roar hung in the room and every man in it remembered, all at once and all the way down, exactly what they were standing next to. Then, into that ringing silence, Barak set his chromed right forearm — the ram, the breaching hardware, the thing built to open bank-vault doors — flat on the steel table, gently, and the table took his weight with a groan of protest, and did not break, and every man in the room understood in his spine that the not breaking was a choice Barak had made about the table and was, at this exact moment, also making about them.

"The terms," Barak said. And just like that the warmth was back, soft and unhurried, as if the roar had been someone else entirely — and the whiplash of it, the kindness returning to the same throat that had just shaken the room, was the most frightening thing the kid had felt all night.

And here was the trick the fixer's file would never capture, because it wasn't in any file — it was in him, the second half of the thing the corps threw away. Barak stayed in the warm voice now, and let it go warmer still, past reassurance, into something that sounded, impossibly, like care. Because the roar was the door, but he had learned — slow, the way he learned everything, and therefore permanently — that fear only opened the room. It did not close a deal. What closed a deal was the warm voice coming back afterward, the offer you made a frightened man to let him walk out whole, delivered in the same gentle rumble that had, thirty seconds ago, nearly stopped his heart. The thing about being the biggest, most obviously lethal object in any room was that you could afford to be generous in a way a smaller, more nervous operator never could — and your generosity landed all the harder for what it followed.

"You keep your original percentage," Barak said, to the frightened kid. "You keep your shooters. You keep your teeth. And you go back to whoever sent you and you tell them the foundry crew honors its contracts, and expects the same, and does not renegotiate — but does not hold a grudge, either, for a man doing his boss's errand." A pause, weighted. "That is a better deal than the one you walked in here to make. You just could not see it, over the chrome."

Sover looked at him for a long moment. Then — slowly, the way you move around a large animal you have decided is not, today, going to eat you — he nodded. And he took the deal, which was the old deal, which was the deal Barak had wanted all along.

They left. Nobody's teeth stayed on the foundry floor. That was, Barak reflected, standing alone again in the dark among the cold dead machines that had been built to do exactly what the corps had built him to do, the entire point.

An angry Goliar coming through the wall ended most negotiations early. Barak had learned to be the wall that didn't come through — the wall that could, and chose, visibly, expensively, in front of everyone, not to. That choice was worth more than any argument. He wore it in grey plate across his chest so no one ever had to wonder whether he had it. But the plate only made men wary. It was the voice that made them loyal — the warm rumble that welcomed them in, the roar that reminded them why they should not test it, and the warmth returning afterward, every time, like a promise kept. Men followed the plate out of fear. They followed the voice because some frightened animal part of them had decided, in the whiplash between the roar and the kindness, that this enormous grey thing had chosen to be gentle with them, and might not always.

The Corp had built him to break things and be pointed. He had kept the being-hard-to-argue-with. He had thrown away the being-pointed.

He ran his own board now. And when the crew sat down to a deal, Barak sat where everyone could see him, and spoke warmly, and welcomed them in — and let them all carry, somewhere behind the ear, the memory of what the warm voice sounded like when it stopped being warm.

It was, the others had learned, the gentlest voice in the Reach. Right up until it wasn't.

*Wren Sable-Corvin — Scout (Hunter) · Changer, Wereraven (Raven lineage)*

*A GHOSTWIRE story · the roofline above the Grid, an hour before the meet*

From up here the Hive looked almost honest.

Wren lay flat on the cold ceramic lip of a Grid-tier maintenance spar, four hundred meters above the street she'd been paid to watch, and let the wind do what it wanted with her coat. She'd found the perch an hour ago the way she found all her perches — she'd gone up as a bird, circled once on the thermal that always rose off the coolant stacks at dusk, and picked the ledge with the cleanest sightline and the worst approach. The worst approach for anyone coming at her. The best approach was always straight down, and straight down was hers alone.

That was the thing the ground people never understood about a Wereraven. They thought the gift was the flying. It wasn't. Anyone with a rotor-drone and a spare afternoon could get height. The gift was the eye — the long, patient, raptor-tuned eye the change had left even in her human face, the eye that could read a man's shoulders from four hundred meters and know, before he knew it himself, that he was about to reach for a gun.

She was reading shoulders now.

The meet was set for a plaza three tiers down, a false-marble apron outside a corp-front noodle house that the fixer had sworn was neutral ground. Wren had stopped believing in neutral ground the first time she'd watched a neutral ground fill up with shooters from a hundred meters up while the marks below smiled and shook hands and had no idea. Neutral ground was a story the ground told itself. From the air there was no such thing — only the ground you could see all of, and the ground you couldn't.

She could see all of this one.

Her crew's client — a nervous Grid-tier data-broker with a briefcase and a bad haircut — was already in position at a café table, doing the small brave things frightened people do to look calm. Two tables over: a couple, too still, not talking, coffees untouched. Corp muscle, plainclothes. Wren had marked them the moment they sat. Marked — she felt the little internal click of it, the study-and-tag her whole trade turned on, the way her attention seized a target and did not let go. She knew the woman's lowest guard now the way she knew the wind. She could put a round through the gap in the man's cheap armor from here, in this wind, and she would not miss, because missing was for people who guessed, and Wren did not guess. Wren watched, and watching, done long enough and patiently enough, stops being a guess and becomes a fact.

But she wasn't here to shoot. She was here to see, and to tell her crew what she saw, half a second before it mattered, which in her experience was the whole of the difference between a job and a funeral.

She keyed her throat-mic. "Two watchers, plainclothes, the couple at your eight," she said, low. "Corp, not street — they've got the posture. They're not here for your client. They're here for the briefcase, which means they already know what's in it, which means your fixer talked." A pause while her long eye swept the plaza edge, the rooflines, the stairwell mouths — the reflex of a creature that has spent its life being small prey to bigger things and has decided, permanently, never to be surprised again. "Third one. Stairwell northeast, hasn't come out yet. He's the closer. When the couple stands, he moves. That's your tell. You've got about nine seconds after they stand."

"Copy," her crew lead breathed. "Can you take the closer?"

Wren considered the stairwell mouth, the angle, the wind, the drop.

"I can do better than take him," she said. "I can make sure nobody has to."

Because here was the second thing the ground people didn't understand, the thing even her own crew sometimes forgot: the Wereraven's real weapon wasn't the rifle laid cold and quiet along the ledge beside her. It was the warning. A shooter who knows he's seen is a shooter doing math instead of shooting. Wren had ended more fights by being visibly, undeniably watching — a single glint of a scope from an impossible height, a shadow with wings crossing the light at the wrong moment — than she had ever ended with the trigger. The corp closer in the stairwell was about to learn that the plaza had a ceiling, and that the ceiling had an eye, and that the eye had already found him.

She let the last of the dusk-light catch her scope, once, deliberately, angled down into the stairwell dark. A flat silver wink. I see you.

In the stairwell, the third man went very still.

The couple did not stand. The briefcase changed hands. Wren's nervous little client walked out of the plaza on his own two legs with his bad haircut and his data intact, and never once looked up, and never knew that the reason he was alive was lying flat on a cold ledge four hundred meters over his head, watching, the way she was always watching, the way the long sight had taught her she would always have to.

When it was done she didn't take the stairs. Scouts who take the stairs get met on the stairs.

She rolled off the ledge into the dark and the drop, and somewhere in the first half-second of falling the change took her — bones going hollow and light, the coat becoming wings, the long human sight folding down into the older, sharper thing it had grown out of — and Wren Sable-Corvin caught the coolant thermal on a black spread of feathers and climbed, unhurried, back up into the only tier of the Hive that was ever really hers.

The high one. The one you could see all of.

![The Dead Frequency](modules/draw-steel-ghostwire/assets/pregens/sabbat-vane.png)

*Sabbat Vane — Technomancer (Sprite-Weaver) · Revenant*

*A GHOSTWIRE story · a coffin-motel cell in the Grid, 03:00*

The dead don't sleep, which is how Sabbat knew it was three in the morning without a clock.

He lay in the coffin-motel cell the way he always lay — flat on his back on the rented slab, hands folded on his chest like something in a mortuary, glowing eyes open to the low ceiling twelve centimeters above his face. He didn't need the sleep. He didn't need the air the cell's cheap scrubber pushed at him either, or the nutrient paste in the dispenser, or any of the small living things the other renters paid for. Deathless Physiology, a corp coroner had called it, back when he'd had a corp and a name and a pulse. Now he just called it quiet. The dead were very quiet. It was the living who could never shut up.

Except tonight the dead were talking.

He'd felt it come on an hour ago — the itch behind the glowing eyes, the pull he'd learned not to fight, the sense of a frequency just below hearing where the net's ghosts drifted. Because here was the thing no coroner had put in the file, the thing Sabbat had discovered the first time he rose from an alley death with his skull full of static: the net had ghosts too. Not metaphors. Not programs. Ghosts — fragments of dead code, orphaned processes, the digital dead who'd been cut loose when their systems were decommissioned and had simply refused, like him, to stop. Most deckers couldn't hear them. Most mages couldn't touch them. But a dead man who'd learned to speak to the recently deceased could, it turned out, speak to the deceased of the machine world just as easily. They were the same congregation. They were his.

He reached up — not with his hands, which stayed folded on his chest — and touched the frequency, and the frequency answered.

"Compile," Sabbat murmured, and out of the dark of the cell a shape unfolded: a Data-sprite, a scrap of half-aware code shaped, by his expectation, like a small pale bird made of drifting numbers. It hung in the air over his coffin-slab and turned its non-face toward him and waited, the way the recently dead always waited on him — patient, incurious, glad of the attention. He'd never had to force a sprite. Other technomancers wrestled the net for its spirits, bribed them, bound them screaming. Sabbat's came willingly. Death recognized death. The ghosts of the machine world looked at the cold glowing-eyed thing on the rented slab and saw, correctly, one of their own.

"There's a man outside my door," Sabbat told the sprite, in the flat unhurried voice of someone who had stopped being afraid of endings a long time ago. "Been there four minutes. Go and see whose he is."

The Data-sprite folded itself thin and slid under the coffin-cell's door into the corridor, and for a moment Sabbat rode its borrowed senses out into the hall — Deep Communion, the mages would call it, though he needed no rig and no deck to do it; the communion was the interface, the way talking to a ghost was the interface for a séance. Through the sprite's eyes he saw the man: cheap armor under a courier's jacket, a fresh corporate SIN, and slaved to his belt a little killware drone still folded up asleep. Not a courier. A cleaner. Someone had finally decided that the dead man who talked to dead code knew too much, and had sent a living man to make him properly dead.

Sabbat almost smiled. It was a common mistake. People saw the rot and the glowing eyes and thought dead meant fragile. They had it exactly backwards.

He compiled the second sprite without rising from the slab — an Attack-sprite this time, a knot of hostile code shaped like a coiled black thing — and then a third, because the Weaver's gift was the congregation, the many, and Sabbat was never more himself than when the ghosts crowded thick around him. Three sprites now, drifting in the dark of a coffin motel, and a fourth compiling, the frequency deepening with each one until the whole cell hummed with the presence of the willing dead.

Out in the corridor the cleaner keyed a lockpick-jack into Sabbat's door.

Sabbat sent the congregation through the wall to meet him — not himself, he stayed folded on his slab, hands on his chest, glowing eyes on the ceiling — just the ghosts, his ghosts, the ones who came when he called because they knew him for kin. The Attack-sprite jacked the cleaner's own killware drone and turned it. The Data-sprite blinded his SIN-reader and his optics at once. The Ward-sprite wrapped Sabbat's cell in a skin of resonance so that even if the man got the door open he'd find nothing his weapons understood how to hurt.

It was over in the time it takes a living heart to beat a dozen times. The cleaner fled — babbling, later, in whatever debrief his corp gave him, about a coffin cell full of ghosts, about a dead thing that hadn't even sat up, about numbers in the dark that moved like birds. Nobody believed him. Nobody ever did. That, too, was Sabbat's protection: he was impossible, and impossible things don't get budgeted for.

When the corridor was empty again Sabbat let the congregation fade — the sprites decompiling one by one, dissolving back into the frequency they'd risen from, going home to the quiet the way he would, someday, when his own unfinished business finally let him rest. He did not know yet what that business was. He'd died in an alley with his purpose already half-erased; recovering it was the long work of his second life. But he knew this much: the dead were patient, and he had all the time that not-dying gave him, and a congregation of ghosts who came when he called.

He folded his hands back on his chest. He fixed his glowing eyes on the ceiling twelve centimeters above his face.

And in the quiet that only the dead really know, Sabbat listened to the frequency below hearing, where his people drifted, and was — in the only way a dead man can be — content.

*Vira Kellis-Nade — Wrench (Drone / Swarm-Master) · Changer, Wererat (Rat lineage)*

*A GHOSTWIRE story · a dead ventilation gallery under the Warrens, mid-run*

She had counted the exits before she counted the enemy. That was the first thing the tunnels taught you, and the tunnels had raised her: always know how you leave before you know why you came.

The job had come the way all her jobs came — through Cassavir's board. Vira had climbed up to the Grid for it, to the dead switching-station the old woman ran like a confessional and a hiring hall at once, all cold relays and a hundred silent lines wired back to a single humming heart. Mama Cassavir "the Switchboard" took clean contracts from above and dirty ones from below and connected the two for a fee, and she wrote nothing down; she just looked at Vira over the hum and said, Somebody's paying to have a thing that lives in your tunnels stop living there. You're the one who knows the tunnels, sweet. She was always smaller than they thought.

She always had one more.

*Kessic Draye — Hacker (Disruptor / offensive decker) · Mutant Human (Aberrant strain)*

*A GHOSTWIRE story · a corp sub-annex on the Grid, the crew stacked at a door they are not supposed to reach*

The others had a plan for the door. Kessic Draye had a plan for the building.

He sat with his back against the corridor wall, three feet from the breach point, and to anyone watching he looked like a corpse propped there to dry — thin, grey-skinned, still, a hood pulled low over a face that even friends found hard to hold a gaze on. A datajack cable ran from the port behind his ear to a scuffed deck in his lap, and his eyes were open and seeing nothing in this room at all. His body was here. Kessic was somewhere else.

He was inside.

"Talk to me, Null," Krow said over the crew-net — the big Cyborg planted in front of Kessic's slumped body like a wall, because that was the arrangement, that was always the arrangement: while the ghost is in the machine, someone guards the meat. A jacked-in decker was a bag of organs with the lights off. Everyone in the crew knew it. Everyone in the crew stood over him for it.

"Give me a second," Kessic said, and his voice came out flat and far away, the voice of a man reading a room he wasn't standing in. "I'm meeting the neighbors."

The sub-annex bloomed around him as a lattice of light — not walls and doors but nodes, every powered thing a glowing knot in the net: the maglocks, the camera runs, the two ceiling turrets folded up in their housings, the four smartguns the corp-sec team downstairs were carrying without knowing their guns had ears. That was the thing the wageslaves never understood about their own gear. Everything talks. Everything on the Grid was wired, and wired meant listening, and listening meant Kessic could lean close and whisper to it in a language it could not refuse to hear.

The outer ICE was cheap. He went through it clean — Intrusion, the break-in that was his daily bread, and it landed crisp on the first pass, no noise, the log staying quiet. He felt the little bank of throughput settle into him as he crossed the threshold, the deep-in-the-system feeling every decker chased: the further in you are, the more you can do. One node became a doorway to the next. He breached the camera run and it opened the door-bank, and the door-bank was slaved to the turret housings, and just like that Kessic was standing — in the only way that mattered — in the middle of everything they thought was theirs.

And nobody knew he was there. That was the whole art of it. Any thug could kick a server. Kessic could stand in the corp's own house with his hand on every light switch and scrub his own footprints as he went, so the Alert board upstairs stayed a calm and lying green. He was the man who owned the heat clock. The one thing the whole hive feared — the rising number, the trace, the moment the system notices — he held in his palm and turned down like a thermostat.

"Cameras are mine," he reported, flat and far. "Doors are mine. Alert's asleep and I'm keeping it that way. You want the room quiet or you want it loud?"

Krow's non-voice, dry as a fuse: "We want it over."

Downstairs, the corp-sec team came up the stair in a textbook stack, four shooters, smartlinked and confident, guns that put a targeting reticle in each man's eye. Confident men with smart guns. Kessic almost felt sorry for them. Almost.

He reached into their smartlinks all at once — Electronic Warfare, the disruptor's hammer, a wide wash of hostile static across every wired weapon in the stairwell — and their reticles died. Just like that. Four men who had trained their whole careers to shoot where the machine told them to, suddenly holding four expensive clubs, their aim gone to a bane, their comms shrieking. Then he did the thing he loved, the thing that was his, the offensive decker's signature cruelty: he did not just blind their guns.

He turned one around.

The lead man's smartgun was the nicest in the stack, and a nice gun is a talkative gun, and Kessic subverted it mid-raise — spoofed its owner-lock, flipped it hostile, and for one bright ugly second the weapon in the corp-sec leader's hands belonged to the grey man upstairs with the cable in his skull. It bucked once, on its own, into the shooter beside its owner. The stack came apart in screaming and confusion, and that was when the crew's own guns spoke, down the compromised hall, into an enemy that no longer trusted the hardware bolted to their own hands.

"Turrets," Krow said.

"Already ours." Kessic had Lockdown on the whole floor now — a five-count of pure control, doors sealing into walls the enemy couldn't open, the two ceiling turrets unfolding from their housings and swiveling to answer his commands, the elevators frozen, the exits that corp-sec wanted turned into a map that only opened for the crew. For as long as he held it, the building was not the corp's building. It was Kessic's. Everyone relying on a system he'd seized moved at a bane, in a house that had quietly, invisibly, changed sides.

He felt the host's ICE come awake then — real ICE, black and biting, a security decker somewhere on a higher floor finally noticing that the sub-annex had a ghost in it. It came for him the way it always came, a lance of hostile code reaching down the wire toward the soft jacked-in brain at the far end. This was the danger. This was the price of being in. If it caught him clean it would ride the cable back to a body slumped in a corridor and stop his heart in it.

But biting Kessic meant biting a man who was already wrong. The ICE hit the taint in him — the aberrant, off-grid strangeness the corps had made when they'd made him, the mutation that let him think in a machine-tongue no clean human brain could — and it hit Aberrant Resilience, the curse that also armored him, and it slid off harder than it should. He felt it as a cold jolt behind his eyes, a wound to nothing. He was still standing in their house.

So he bit back. The security decker was wired — of course he was, they always were — and a wired enemy was the one target Kessic could actually hurt with his own hand. He reached down the trace the man had opened and sent the biofeedback the other way, a feedback spike straight into an unguarded skull, and somewhere on a higher floor a man in a very expensive chair jerked and went slack and stopped noticing anything at all for a while.

"Clear up here," Kessic said. "They've lost the room. They just don't all know it yet."

It was over in ninety seconds, the way it was supposed to be when he did his job right — no alarm ever tripped, no reinforcement ever called, because the man who would have called them was a decker Kessic had put to sleep and a security system Kessic had owned. The crew walked out through doors that opened only for them and closed like they'd never been touched.

He came back to his body last, the way he always did — the pull up the cable, the sudden weight of a grey and aching frame, the corridor rushing back in around him. Krow was still standing over him, hadn't moved, a wall between the ghost and the world.

Kessic pulled the jack, coiled the cable, and got up without a word, because there was nothing to say that the log wouldn't have said better if he'd let it keep any record at all. He hadn't. That was the point.

Let them find nothing. Let them find no alarm, no trace, no wrongness — nothing but their own guns turned the wrong way and a green board that had lied to them all night. Let them stand in a room they thought was theirs and never understand it had belonged to someone else the whole time.

The best runs were the ones the target never knew had happened.

Kessic Draye was very, very good at making sure they never knew.

Kessic pulled the jack, coiled the cable, and got up without a word, because there was nothing to say that the log wouldn't have said better if he'd let it keep any record at all. He hadn't. That was the point.

Let them find nothing. Let them find no alarm, no trace, no wrongness — nothing but their own guns turned the wrong way and a green board that had lied to them all night. Let them stand in a room they thought was theirs and never understand it had belonged to someone else the whole time.

The best runs were the ones the target never knew had happened.

Kessic Draye was very, very good at making sure they never knew.
